title: Did Baby Hanuman Swallow the Sun?
status: DRAFT v1 — CE Kishkindha 4.65 and Uttara 7.35-36 read; review before posting
source: Valmiki Ramayana, Kishkindha Kanda 4(65) and Uttara Kanda 7(35-36) (Critical Edition; vulgate 4.66, 7.35-36)
avoid: any disrespect to the Hanuman Chalisa: it is a hymn of devotion; we only say Valmiki tells the episode differently
pain or injury detail: the jaw breaking is shown as a flash and a gentle fall, no wound
the curse that made him forget his powers (that is A38, the follow-up)
saying he 'reached and grabbed' the sun as fact in Kishkindha: there he is pushed back; only Uttara has him reach the sun's chariot
naming the Chalisa's author (traditional attribution only); quote the line itself, chaupai 18
verify_note: CE 4.65.19: as a child he saw the rising sun, wanted to seize it as a fruit, and leapt into the sky. 4.65.20: after 300 yojanas, driven back by its radiance, not dejected. 4.65.21-22: Indra hurls the thunderbolt; on a mountain peak his left jaw breaks; hence the name Hanuman. (Narrated by Jambavan to Hanuman, 4.65.1-2.) CE 7.35.23-24: sees the rising sun like hibiscus, flies up wanting the fruit. 7.35.28-30: Vayu keeps him cool; he comes near the sun; the sun does not burn him. 7.35.31-44: meets Rahu on the sun's chariot; chases Rahu, then Airavata ('this too is a great fruit'). 7.35.46-47: Indra's thunderbolt; falls on the mountain; left jaw broken. 7.36.11: Indra: named Hanuman because his jaw (hanu) was injured. No swallowing of the sun in either telling. Hanuman Chalisa: 'जुग सहस्र जोजन पर भानू। लील्यो ताहि मधुर फल जानू॥'
caption: Many of us grew up singing that baby Hanuman swallowed the sun, thinking it was a sweet fruit. Valmiki tells this story twice. In the Kishkindha Kanda, Jambavan tells Hanuman that as a child he leapt at the rising sun, flew three hundred yojanas, and was pushed back by its heat, without losing heart. In the Uttara Kanda, the Wind god keeps him cool, he reaches the sun's chariot, then chases Rahu and even Indra's elephant Airavata. In both, Indra's thunderbolt breaks his left jaw, and that is how he got his name: Hanuman. Neither telling has him swallow the sun. That comes from a beautiful line of the Hanuman Chalisa (chaupai 18): “Jug sahasra jojan par bhanu, leelyo tahi madhur phal janu”, the sun, yug-sahasra yojanas away, swallowed as a sweet fruit. We sing it with devotion; Valmiki tells it differently.

score.prompt: Wondrous Indian dawn underscore, instrumental only, built to sit under a spoken voice. Opens with a soft bansuri flute and a warm tanpura drone, gentle and curious like a child at sunrise; a light, playful tabla and frame-drum rhythm at about 92 BPM lifts into a soaring feeling of flight with rising strings; around the middle a sudden sharp thunder-like percussion hit and a held, tense low drone; then a warm, tender resolution with flute and soft strings that ends calm and devotional. Sparse mid-range, no vocals, no lead melody fighting the narration, crisp modern film production.

shots.en: Valmiki tells this story twice. First, Jambavan tells it to Hanuman himself.

पहली बार, जाम्बवान स्वयं हनुमान को सुनाते हैं।

shots.en: Little Hanuman sees the rising sun, thinks it's a fruit, and leaps into the sky.

shots.en: He flies three hundred yojanas. The sun's blaze pushes him back, but he doesn't lose heart.
units: तीन सौ योजन तक उड़ते हैं।

shots.en: There he meets Rahu, and then Indra's elephant Airavata. That looks like a fruit to him too!

shots.en: Indra hurls his thunderbolt. The child falls on a mountain, and his left jaw breaks.

claims.claim: Valmiki tells the episode twice: Jambavan to Hanuman (Kishkindha) and Agastya to Rama (Uttara)
As a child he saw the rising sun, thought it a fruit, and leapt into the sky
After 300 yojanas, driven back by the sun's radiance, he was not dejected
In the Uttara telling, Vayu keeps him cool, the sun does not burn him, and he comes near the sun
He meets Rahu on the sun's chariot, chases him, then runs at Airavata thinking it a great fruit
Indra's thunderbolt strikes him; he falls on a mountain and his left jaw breaks
He is named Hanuman because his jaw (hanu) was injured
Neither telling has him swallow the sun
The swallowing comes from the Hanuman Chalisa: 'जुग सहस्र जोजन पर भानू। लील्यो ताहि मधुर फल जानू॥'
Opening śloka: “Then, on a mountain peak, your left jaw was broken. That is why you are called Hanuman.”
